lesson.title: The Data Science Lifecycle & Problem Framing
objectives: Explain what a data scientist does and how the role differs from a data analyst and an ML engineer.
Describe each stage of the data science lifecycle (CRISP-DM style) and what it produces.
Translate a vague business question into a measurable data science problem.
Explain why most project time goes into data work rather than modelling.
Answer lifecycle and project-walkthrough interview questions with a clear structure.
lesson.definition: Data science is the practice of turning data into decisions using statistics, programming and domain knowledge. The data science lifecycle is the repeatable sequence a project follows: define the problem, collect data, clean it, explore it, build models, evaluate them against the business goal, deploy the result and monitor it in production. The lifecycle is iterative: findings in a later stage often send you back to an earlier one.

theory.heading: What a data scientist actually does
theory.body: A data scientist sits between business questions and data. A data analyst mostly describes what happened (dashboards, reports, SQL), an ML engineer mostly builds and scales production systems, and a data scientist frames questions, runs statistical analyses and experiments, and builds predictive models. In Indian product companies, banks and startups the boundaries blur, so interviewers test all three skills: SQL and pandas for data work, statistics for inference and machine learning for prediction.
points: Descriptive: what happened? (reports, EDA)
Diagnostic: why did it happen? (segmentation, hypothesis tests)
Predictive: what will happen? (machine-learning models)
Prescriptive: what should we do? (experiments, optimisation, decision rules)

theory.heading: Stages of the lifecycle
theory.body: CRISP-DM (Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining) is the best-known framework: business understanding, data understanding, data preparation, modelling, evaluation and deployment. Modern teams add monitoring because models degrade when the world changes. Each stage has a concrete output, which is what interviewers want you to name.
points: Define: business goal, success metric, constraints (e.g. reduce churn by 5% within a quarter).
Collect: identify sources (databases, logs, APIs, surveys) and pull a dataset.
Clean: fix types, duplicates, missing values and inconsistent labels.
Explore (EDA): distributions, relationships, data quality issues, early hypotheses.
Model: features, baseline, candidate algorithms, tuning.
Evaluate: offline metrics plus business impact; check fairness and leakage.
Deploy and monitor: serve predictions, track drift and performance, retrain.

theory.heading: Problem framing: the most underrated step
theory.body: A model that answers the wrong question is worthless however accurate it is. Framing turns 'customers are leaving' into a precise target ('predict whether an active subscriber cancels in the next 30 days'), a unit of prediction (one row per customer per month), a metric that reflects cost (recall on churners at a fixed contact budget) and a decision the prediction drives (who receives a retention offer). Framing also decides whether you need machine learning at all: sometimes a SQL rule or a dashboard solves the problem.
points: Define the target variable and the prediction time point precisely.
Choose a metric aligned with business cost, not just accuracy.
Start with a simple baseline (rule, average, last value) to beat.
Agree on how the output will be used before building anything.

theory.heading: Why the lifecycle is iterative
theory.body: Surveys of practitioners consistently report that data collection and cleaning take the majority of project time. EDA may reveal that the target is mislabelled, evaluation may expose leakage, and monitoring may show drift that forces new data collection. Interviewers like candidates who describe these loops honestly instead of a straight line from data to model.
points: Bad data found in EDA sends you back to collection or cleaning.
Poor evaluation results may mean the problem framing was wrong.
Drift found in monitoring triggers retraining or redesign.

theory.heading: Advantages and limitations of a process framework
theory.body: A lifecycle gives teams a shared vocabulary, makes projects auditable and stops people jumping straight to modelling. Its limitation is that it can become bureaucratic; small analyses do not need every stage formally. The skill is knowing which stages carry the most risk for a particular project and spending time there.
points: Advantage: structure, reproducibility and easier communication with stakeholders.
Advantage: forces success criteria to be agreed early.
Limitation: real projects loop and overlap; the stages are not strictly sequential.
Limitation: CRISP-DM says little about MLOps, which modern teams add.

example.title: Framing a churn problem for a telecom company
example.body: Business ask: 'Too many prepaid users are leaving.' Framed problem: for each active user on the 1st of the month, predict whether they will not recharge in the next 30 days, using only data available up to that date. Metric: recall among the top 10% highest-risk users, because the retention team can call only that many. Baseline: flag users whose recharge amount dropped by more than 50% last month. The code shows the framing written down as a checklist that the team agrees on before any modelling.

code.source:
problem = {
    'business_goal': 'Reduce prepaid churn by 5% this quarter',
    'target': 'no recharge in the 30 days after the snapshot date',
    'unit': 'one row per active user per monthly snapshot',
    'features_cutoff': 'only data available before the snapshot date',
    'metric': 'recall in the top 10% risk scores (call-centre capacity)',
    'baseline': 'recharge amount dropped by more than 50% last month',
    'action': 'retention offer for the top 10% each month',
}
for key, value in problem.items():
    print(f'{key:16}: {value}')

interview.question: Walk me through the stages of a data science project.
interview.answer: Define the business problem and success metric, collect data, clean and prepare it, explore it (EDA), engineer features and build models starting from a baseline, evaluate on held-out data against the business metric, deploy, and monitor for drift with periodic retraining. The process is iterative.
interview.explanation: Name a concrete output for each stage and stress iteration. Strong candidates illustrate it with one of their own projects rather than reciting CRISP-DM.

interview.question: How is a data scientist different from a data analyst and an ML engineer?
interview.answer: An analyst focuses on describing and reporting what happened, mainly with SQL and dashboards. A data scientist frames questions, runs statistical analyses and experiments and builds predictive models. An ML engineer focuses on putting models into reliable, scalable production systems.
interview.explanation: Show you understand the overlap: data scientists still write SQL and must think about deployment. Avoid sounding dismissive of other roles.

interview.question: A manager says 'use AI to reduce customer complaints'. How do you start?
interview.answer: Ask clarifying questions: what counts as a complaint, which channel, the current baseline and the goal. Then decide the decision the model supports, for example routing tickets or predicting which orders will cause complaints, define the target and metric, check what data exists, and propose a simple baseline before any complex model.
interview.explanation: Interviewers test whether you jump to algorithms. Clarify, define a measurable target and tie it to an action.

interview.question: Why do you build a baseline model?
interview.answer: A baseline, such as predicting the mean, the majority class or a simple rule, sets the minimum performance a model must beat. It exposes whether the problem is learnable, catches evaluation bugs and tells the business how much value the complex model adds.
interview.explanation: Mention that a surprisingly strong baseline is common, and that if a complex model barely beats it, the simpler solution may be the right one to ship.

interview.question: Your model had 92% offline accuracy but business metrics did not improve after launch. What could be wrong?
interview.answer: Possible causes: the metric was misaligned (accuracy on an imbalanced target), data leakage inflated offline results, training data differs from production data (skew or drift), the predictions were not acted on correctly, or the target did not represent the business outcome. Investigate by comparing offline and online feature distributions, re-checking the split and running a controlled A/B test.
interview.explanation: This advanced question checks lifecycle thinking end to end. Structure the answer by stage: framing, data, evaluation, deployment.

lesson.title: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
objectives: Choose the right built-in structure (list, tuple, dict, set) for a data task and explain the time complexity.
Write list, dict and set comprehensions and generator expressions for data transformations.
Read and parse CSV data safely with the csv module, including quoted fields.
Explain mutability, references and copying, a common source of data bugs.
Answer Python-for-data interview questions confidently.
lesson.definition: Python is the main language of data science because it combines readable syntax with a huge ecosystem (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch). Before those libraries, interviewers check core Python: built-in data structures, comprehensions, functions, file handling and the difference between mutable and immutable objects. These skills decide whether your pandas code is correct and efficient.

theory.heading: Built-in data structures and when to use them
theory.body: Lists are ordered, mutable sequences, good for row-like data you append to. Tuples are immutable and hashable, so they can be dictionary keys (for example a (city, month) group key). Dictionaries map keys to values with average O(1) lookup, the basis of grouping and counting. Sets store unique items with O(1) membership tests, ideal for deduplication and 'have I seen this ID?' checks.
points: list: x in my_list is O(n); avoid it inside loops over large data.
set/dict: membership and lookup are O(1) on average because they use hashing.
tuple: immutable, hashable, lightweight records and composite keys.
collections.Counter and defaultdict simplify counting and grouping.

theory.heading: Comprehensions and generators
theory.body: A comprehension builds a new collection from an iterable in one readable expression: [x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]. Dict and set comprehensions work the same way. A generator expression uses parentheses and yields items lazily, so sum(x for x in big_file) processes a huge file without loading it into memory. Interviewers often ask you to rewrite a loop as a comprehension or explain why a generator saves memory.
points: List comprehension: eager, builds the full list in memory.
Generator expression: lazy, one item at a time, can be consumed only once.
Keep comprehensions simple; nested logic is clearer as a loop.

theory.heading: Mutability, references and copying
theory.body: Python variables are names bound to objects. b = a for a list does not copy it: both names point to the same list, so changing b changes a. copy() or a slice makes a shallow copy (inner objects are still shared) and copy.deepcopy copies everything. A classic bug is a mutable default argument, def f(x, acc=[]), which is created once and shared across calls. The same idea appears in pandas, where a slice may be a view or a copy.
points: Immutable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset.
Mutable: list, dict, set and most user-defined objects.
Use None as a default and create the list inside the function.

theory.heading: Reading data files correctly
theory.body: Splitting lines on commas breaks as soon as a field contains a quoted comma such as "Rao, S". The csv module handles quoting, and csv.DictReader maps each row to the header names. Real data also has blanks, wrong types and inconsistent case, so parsing code should validate each field, count the rows it rejects and normalise text (strip spaces, standardise case).
points: Use with open(path, newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f: for files.
Wrap type conversion in try/except and count bad rows rather than crashing.
Normalise categories ('pune', 'Pune ') before grouping.

theory.heading: Functions, lambdas and sorting
theory.body: Small reusable functions keep data code testable. Lambdas are handy as keys: sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r['score'], r['name'])) sorts by score descending, then name ascending, a pattern used constantly for ranking with tie-breaks. Built-ins such as zip, enumerate, any, all, min and max with key= cover many interview tasks without extra libraries.
points: Negating a numeric key reverses its order inside a tuple key.
sorted() returns a new list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
Python's sort is stable, so equal keys keep their original order.

example.title: Grouping exam scores by city in pure Python
example.body: This is the core of a groupby without pandas: parse rows, normalise the grouping key, collect values in a dictionary and compute an aggregate. The same pattern underlies pandas df.groupby('city')['score'].mean().

takeaways: Use dicts and sets for O(1) lookups; avoid repeated 'in list' checks on large data.
Comprehensions are concise; generators save memory for large streams.
Assignment never copies a list or dict; know shallow versus deep copy.
Never use a mutable default argument.
Parse CSV with the csv module, validate fields and count rejected rows.
Tuple sort keys with negation give multi-level ranking with tie-breaks.

interview.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable. Because tuples are immutable they are hashable (if their items are), so they can be dictionary keys or set members, and they signal fixed records such as (lat, lon).
interview.explanation: Add the practical use: tuples as composite group keys. Mentioning hashability shows deeper understanding than 'one uses brackets'.

interview.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
interview.answer: A set is a hash table: Python hashes the item and jumps to its bucket, giving O(1) average time. A list must be scanned element by element, which is O(n).
interview.explanation: Give a data example: deduplicating 10 million user IDs with a list inside a loop becomes O(n²).

interview.question: What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
interview.answer: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory immediately. A generator expression produces items lazily on demand, uses constant memory and can be iterated only once.
interview.explanation: Mention when to prefer each: generators for streaming large files or feeding sum()/max(), lists when you need indexing or several passes.

interview.question: What happens with def add(item, bucket=[]) when called twice?
interview.answer: The default list is created once when the function is defined, so both calls append to the same list and the second call sees the first item. Use bucket=None and create a new list inside the function.
interview.explanation: This is a favourite trick question; explain the reason (defaults evaluated at definition time), not just the fix.

interview.question: Explain shallow versus deep copy and why it matters in data work.
interview.answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares the inner objects; a deep copy recursively copies everything. If you shallow-copy a list of dicts and modify a dict, the original changes too, silently corrupting data used elsewhere.
interview.explanation: Link it to pandas: df2 = df does not copy; use df.copy() before modifying, which also avoids SettingWithCopy problems.

quiz.question: What does this list aliasing example print?
quiz.explanation: b = a binds a second name to the same list object, so appending through b also changes a. Its length becomes 4.

quiz.question: Which structure gives O(1) average-time membership checks for deduplicating user IDs?
quiz.explanation: Sets are hash-based, so 'id in seen' is O(1) on average, while lists and tuples require a linear scan.

quiz.question: You need the total of a numeric column from a 20 GB log file on a laptop with 8 GB RAM. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: sum(parse(line) for line in file) using a generator
Read all lines into a list first, then sum
Convert the file to a single string and split it
Load it into a dictionary keyed by line number
quiz.explanation: A generator processes one line at a time with constant memory; building a list of all lines would exceed RAM.

quiz.question: In what order does this sorted() call print the names?
quiz.code:
rows = [('b', 5), ('a', 5), ('c', 9)]
print([r[0] for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-r[1], r[0]))])
quiz.explanation: The key sorts by score descending (negated) then name ascending: c (9) first, then a and b, which tie on 5 and are ordered alphabetically.

quiz.question: Why is line.split(',') a risky way to parse the CSV line '"Rao, S",Hyderabad,90'?
options: It produces four fields because the comma inside quotes is also split
It removes the quotes but keeps the fields correct
split() only works on files, not strings
quiz.explanation: Plain split ignores quoting and breaks 'Rao, S' into two fields. The csv module understands quoted fields.

questions.topic: The Data Science Lifecycle & Problem Framing
questions.question: Why do you build a baseline model?
questions.answer: A baseline, such as predicting the mean, the majority class or a simple rule, sets the minimum performance a model must beat. It exposes whether the problem is learnable, catches evaluation bugs and tells the business how much value the complex model adds.
questions.explanation: Mention that a surprisingly strong baseline is common, and that if a complex model barely beats it, the simpler solution may be the right one to ship.

questions.topic: The Data Science Lifecycle & Problem Framing
questions.question: Your model had 92% offline accuracy but business metrics did not improve after launch. What could be wrong?
questions.answer: Possible causes: the metric was misaligned (accuracy on an imbalanced target), data leakage inflated offline results, training data differs from production data (skew or drift), the predictions were not acted on correctly, or the target did not represent the business outcome. Investigate by comparing offline and online feature distributions, re-checking the split and running a controlled A/B test.
questions.explanation: This advanced question checks lifecycle thinking end to end. Structure the answer by stage: framing, data, evaluation, deployment.

questions.topic: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
questions.answer: A list is mutable and a tuple is immutable. Because tuples are immutable they are hashable (if their items are), so they can be dictionary keys or set members, and they signal fixed records such as (lat, lon).
questions.explanation: Add the practical use: tuples as composite group keys. Mentioning hashability shows deeper understanding than 'one uses brackets'.

questions.topic: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
questions.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
questions.answer: A set is a hash table: Python hashes the item and jumps to its bucket, giving O(1) average time. A list must be scanned element by element, which is O(n).
questions.explanation: Give a data example: deduplicating 10 million user IDs with a list inside a loop becomes O(n²).

questions.topic: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
questions.question: What is the difference between a list comprehension and a generator expression?
questions.answer: A list comprehension builds the whole list in memory immediately. A generator expression produces items lazily on demand, uses constant memory and can be iterated only once.
questions.explanation: Mention when to prefer each: generators for streaming large files or feeding sum()/max(), lists when you need indexing or several passes.

questions.topic: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
questions.question: What happens with def add(item, bucket=[]) when called twice?
questions.answer: The default list is created once when the function is defined, so both calls append to the same list and the second call sees the first item. Use bucket=None and create a new list inside the function.
questions.explanation: This is a favourite trick question; explain the reason (defaults evaluated at definition time), not just the fix.

questions.topic: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
questions.question: Explain shallow versus deep copy and why it matters in data work.
questions.answer: A shallow copy creates a new outer container but shares the inner objects; a deep copy recursively copies everything. If you shallow-copy a list of dicts and modify a dict, the original changes too, silently corrupting data used elsewhere.
questions.explanation: Link it to pandas: df2 = df does not copy; use df.copy() before modifying, which also avoids SettingWithCopy problems.

days.title: The Data Science Lifecycle & Problem Framing
days.focus: Data science is the practice of turning data into decisions using statistics, programming and domain knowledge. The data science lifecycle is the repeatable sequence a project follows: define the problem, collect data, clean it, explore it, build models, evaluate them against the business goal, deploy the result and monitor it in production. The lifecycle is iterative: findings in a later stage often send you back to an earlier one.
objectives: Explain what a data scientist does and how the role differs from a data analyst and an ML engineer.
Describe each stage of the data science lifecycle (CRISP-DM style) and what it produces.
Translate a vague business question into a measurable data science problem.
Explain why most project time goes into data work rather than modelling.
Answer lifecycle and project-walkthrough interview questions with a clear structure.
days.assignment: Read N task log lines of the form stage,hours. Valid stages, in lifecycle order, are define, collect, clean, explore, model, evaluate, deploy and monitor (case-insensitive). Ignore a line if it does not have exactly two comma-separated parts, the stage is unknown, or hours is not a number or is negative. Print the total hours and percentage share of every stage that appears, in lifecycle order, then the bottleneck stage (most hours; on a tie, the earliest stage), the stages that never appear, and how many lines were ignored. If no line is valid, print 'No valid tasks' instead of the stage lines and the bottleneck.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: The lifecycle is define, collect, clean, explore, model, evaluate, deploy and monitor, and it loops.
Problem framing (target, unit, metric, decision) matters more than the choice of algorithm.
Always build a simple baseline first; a model must beat it to be worth deploying.
Data preparation usually takes most of the project time.
Evaluation must connect offline metrics to business impact.
Deployment is not the end: monitoring catches drift and decay.

days.title: Python for Data Science: Core Structures, Comprehensions & Files
days.focus: Python is the main language of data science because it combines readable syntax with a huge ecosystem (NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch). Before those libraries, interviewers check core Python: built-in data structures, comprehensions, functions, file handling and the difference between mutable and immutable objects. These skills decide whether your pandas code is correct and efficient.
objectives: Choose the right built-in structure (list, tuple, dict, set) for a data task and explain the time complexity.
Write list, dict and set comprehensions and generator expressions for data transformations.
Read and parse CSV data safely with the csv module, including quoted fields.
Explain mutability, references and copying, a common source of data bugs.
Answer Python-for-data interview questions confidently.
days.assignment: Read a CSV with header name,city,score from standard input. Strip spaces from names and cities and convert cities to title case. Skip a row (and count it) if the score is not a number or the name or city is empty. For each city in alphabetical order print the count, average score and the top student (highest score; ties broken by name alphabetically). Then print the overall top student with the same tie rule, and the number of skipped rows. If no row is valid, print 'No valid rows' instead of the overall line.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Use dicts and sets for O(1) lookups; avoid repeated 'in list' checks on large data.
Comprehensions are concise; generators save memory for large streams.
Assignment never copies a list or dict; know shallow versus deep copy.
Never use a mutable default argument.
Parse CSV with the csv module, validate fields and count rejected rows.
Tuple sort keys with negation give multi-level ranking with tie-breaks.
